items.explanation: The Compromise calmed the immediate crisis with Senate balance and the 36°30' line, but the settlement did not hold -- the Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854 repealed that line, reopening the fight over slavery's expansion. A deal undone within a generation did not resolve the crisis, whatever the truce mechanism, Clay's reputation, or the quiet decades suggest.
items.fact_source: Missouri Compromise (1820); Tallmadge Amendment debate (1819); Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854) repeal of the 36°30' line; Clay's 'Great Compromiser' reputation.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Senate balance was the mechanism of the truce, not proof that the underlying conflict was settled.
option_explanations.B: Right. Repealing the Compromise's core restriction shows the supposed 'resolution' failed within a generation.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. This judges an 1820 bargain by an abolition standard its makers never set; the question is whether the crisis was resolved, not whether slavery ended.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Decades without war do not equal a resolved crisis -- the nullification fight and the gag-rule battles of the 1830s show the conflict kept burning.

options: (A) Missouri entered the Union as a slave state while Maine entered as a free state, keeping the Senate evenly balanced, which proves the crisis was settled
(B) Congress repealed the Compromise's 36°30' restriction on slavery's expansion in the Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854
(C) The Compromise failed because it did not abolish slavery, and only abolition could have resolved the crisis
(D) The nation avoided war over slavery until 1861, which shows the Compromise kept the crisis resolved for forty years
items.stem: A historian argues that the Missouri Compromise of 1820 resolved the sectional crisis over the expansion of slavery. Which additional evidence would most call that argument into question?

items.explanation: The claim is about what most free Black northerners believed, so the test is evidence from them. A mass protest of thousands in 1817 and sustained attacks on the society in Black newspapers directly contradict the idea of broad Black support. (A) confuses the society's sales pitch with its audience's opinion. (B) stretches a few leaders' views into a whole population's. (C) answers a different question -- what happened in Liberia in 1847 says nothing about Black opinion in the 1820s and 1830s.
items.fact_source: Philadelphia protest against colonization, January 1817 (about 3,000 at Bethel Church); Freedom's Journal (1827) opposed ACS colonization; ACS founded 1816.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The society's published appeals show what it wanted people to believe, not what free Black northerners actually believed. Stated good intentions are not evidence of anyone else's opinion.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. A few Black leaders' interest in emigration cannot be stretched into the views of most free Black northerners, and independent emigrationism was not the same as supporting the ACS.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. What happened in Liberia in 1847 does not answer what free Black northerners believed in the 1820s and 1830s -- a later outcome is not evidence of earlier opinion.
option_explanations.D: Correct. It supplies direct evidence from free Black northerners themselves -- a mass protest and sustained Black newspaper opposition -- which directly undercuts the claim that most supported the society.

options: (A) The society's published appeals described colonization as a blessing for free Black people, so its stated good intentions prove that Black northerners supported the plan.
(B) A few prominent Black leaders favored emigration to Africa, which shows that the colonization idea had genuine appeal among free Black people generally.
(C) Liberia declared its independence in 1847, which proves that the society's plan eventually succeeded.
(D) In 1817 thousands of free Black Philadelphians protested colonization, and Black newspapers in the 1820s denounced the society as a removal scheme.
items.stem: A historian argues that in the 1820s and 1830s most free Black people in the North supported the American Colonization Society's plan to settle them in Liberia. Which evidence most undermines that argument?

items.explanation: The doctrine was a bold statement, but the United States had only a small navy and army in the 1820s and could not have stopped a determined European power on its own. Britain's Royal Navy — motivated by British trade interests in Latin America — was the real deterrent, which means the doctrine's force depended on a power the United States did not control. European interest in the hemisphere had not vanished either: Russia was pressing claims in the Pacific Northwest.
items.fact_source: Monroe Doctrine, December 2, 1823; Britain's Canning proposed a joint declaration (August 1823); Russia's Ukase of 1821 asserted Pacific Northwest claims; U.S. Navy small in the 1820s.

option_explanations.A: Right. It qualifies the claim by showing the United States lacked the force to back its words — British sea power, not American power, did the deterring in the 1820s.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. It treats the doctrine as the single cause of everything that followed and overstates the outcome — European powers did intervene in the hemisphere again, as France did in Mexico in the 1860s.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. It projects later presidents' uses of the doctrine backward onto 1823. How the doctrine was used decades later does not show what power the United States held when it was proclaimed.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. European powers still had real interests in the Americas — Russia's 1821 claims in the Pacific Northwest were one of the reasons Monroe issued the message at all.

options: (A) The United States had only a small navy in the 1820s; it was Britain's Royal Navy, not American force, that truly discouraged European intervention.
(B) Because no European power ever again established a colony in the Americas, the doctrine alone ended European imperialism in the entire Western Hemisphere.
(C) Later presidents used the doctrine to justify sending troops abroad, which proves it gave the United States enforcement power from 1823.
(D) Spain's empire was already collapsing, so by the 1820s no European power had any interest left in the Americas.
items.stem: A historian claims that the Monroe Doctrine made the United States the dominant power in the Western Hemisphere beginning in the 1820s. Which consideration most qualifies that claim?

stimulus.text: President James Monroe's 1823 message to Congress warned European powers against further colonization or intervention in the Americas (paraphrased).

items.explanation: The claim overstates the change. Property requirements for white men did fall away in most states by the 1840s, and turnout surged — but 'fully democratic' ignores that women, enslaved people, and most free Black men could not vote at all. The expansion was real but bounded: it democratized politics for white men, not for all Americans.
items.fact_source: White manhood suffrage largely achieved by the 1840s (most states dropped property qualifications; Rhode Island 1842); women, enslaved people, and most free Black men excluded (New York's 1821 constitution kept a $250 property requirement for Black voters).

option_explanations.A: Wrong. High turnout shows that many of those allowed to vote did so; it does not show that everyone was allowed. Participation by the included says nothing about the excluded.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. It credits one man with the whole change. Property requirements were already falling before Jackson took office and kept falling after — legislatures, not Jackson alone, made those changes.
option_explanations.C: Right. It accepts the real expansion to white men while naming the groups still shut out, which is exactly where 'fully democratic' fails.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. It reverses the regional pattern: most eastern states had dropped property qualifications by the 1840s, and western states were not the lone holdouts of democracy.

options: (A) It is accurate: voter turnout reached record levels in 1840, which proves that all Americans could participate in politics.
(B) It is accurate: Andrew Jackson personally ended property requirements for voting, making him the single cause of American democracy.
(C) It overstates the case: property barriers for white men largely fell, but women, enslaved people, and most free Black men could not vote.
(D) It is inaccurate: eastern states kept property requirements for voting until after the Civil War, while only western states democratized.
items.stem: A historian writes: 'By the 1840s, Jacksonian democracy had made the United States a fully democratic nation.' Which evaluation of this claim is most accurate?

items.explanation: A veto message is political persuasion, not an economic study. Jackson issued it in 1832 while running for reelection, and Henry Clay's supporters had forced the recharter vote precisely to make the Bank a campaign issue. Because its purpose was to win votes, it asserts harm without offering any lending or price figures — so a historian needs other evidence to measure the Bank's real effects, and should not discard the source but recognize what it can and cannot show. Congress sustained the veto; no override ever occurred.
items.fact_source: Bank veto message, July 10, 1832 (election-year; printed in newspapers as campaign material); Senate sustained the veto — no override.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The message was printed in newspapers and circulated nationwide as campaign material, so its audience included voters, not just Congress. The limit is its persuasive purpose, not its addressee.
option_explanations.B: Right. It identifies the source's election-year purpose and the specific gap — no economic data — that limits its use for measuring the Bank's actual effects on borrowers.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. A source's bias limits what it can prove; it does not make every claim false or the source useless. Historians use biased sources by asking what each source is fit to show.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Congress sustained Jackson's veto; no override occurred. The recharter simply died, and Jackson won reelection in 1832.

options: (A) The message was addressed only to members of Congress, so it reveals nothing about how ordinary Americans viewed the Bank.
(B) Written as an election-year appeal against the Bank, it offers accusations but no loan or price figures, so it cannot by itself establish the Bank's economic effects.
(C) Jackson's well-known hostility to all banks and paper money means every claim in the message is false, so historians should ignore this source entirely.
(D) Congress overrode the veto within weeks of its delivery in July 1832, which shows that even the lawmakers who received it rejected the message's claims about the Bank.
items.stem: A historian wants to use this veto message to measure how the Bank of the United States actually affected ordinary borrowers. What most limits the message for that purpose?

stimulus.text: President Andrew Jackson's 1832 veto of the bill rechartering the Bank of the United States: "It is to be regretted that the rich and powerful too often bend the acts of government to their selfish purposes."

items.explanation: The Offering was written by operatives, but it appeared with the mill companies' approval and was created partly to answer public criticism of factory life. A publication designed to defend the mill system will naturally emphasize its pleasant side, so its cheerful picture cannot be taken as a neutral record of conditions. The early Lowell workforce was also native-born farm daughters from New England, not immigrants.
items.fact_source: Lowell Offering published 1840-1845 with company oversight; early Lowell operatives were native-born New England farm daughters; Irish immigration to the mills grew later in the 1840s.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The problem is not that it shows only one side's viewpoint — the problem is that the cheerful side shown served the companies' interest in defending the mill system, since the magazine needed their approval.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Lowell Offering ran from 1840 to 1845, squarely during the Lowell system's operation, so its timing is not the issue.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The early Lowell operatives were native-born New England farm daughters; large-scale Irish immigration to the mills came later, in the late 1840s and 1850s.
option_explanations.D: Right. It identifies the editorial situation — company approval and a defensive purpose aimed at critics — that limits the magazine's use as a neutral record of working conditions.

options: (A) Because the articles were written by mill workers themselves, the magazine gives only the workers' viewpoint and ignores the mill owners' perspective entirely.
(B) The magazine was published in the 1840s, after the Lowell system had already declined, so it describes conditions that no longer existed.
(C) The operatives who wrote for it were Irish immigrants, whose experiences differed from those of native-born workers.
(D) The magazine appeared with the companies' approval to answer public criticism of factory life, so its cheerful picture served the companies' interests too.
items.stem: A historian wants to use this magazine to describe daily working conditions in the Lowell mills. What most limits the magazine for that purpose?

stimulus.text: An 1840s issue of the Lowell Offering, a magazine written by women working in Lowell's textile mills, describes the boardinghouses as comfortable and mill work as compatible with education and self-improvement (paraphrased).

items.explanation: The immediate fight was over the tariffs of 1828 and 1832, which South Carolina's Ordinance of Nullification explicitly named — so the tariff interpretation is not wrong about the trigger. But South Carolina's leaders, led by Calhoun, feared that conceding Congress's power to impose protective tariffs would concede its power over slavery itself. Treating it as either-or misses how the tariff fight was, for its leaders, also a rehearsal for defending slavery.
items.fact_source: South Carolina Exposition and Protest (1828, Calhoun anonymously); Tariffs of 1828 and 1832; Ordinance of Nullification (November 1832); Force Bill and Compromise Tariff (1833).

option_explanations.A: Wrong. What a document names is its stated grievance, not necessarily its deepest motive. Reading the ordinance literally rules out the slavery fear that Calhoun and others expressed privately.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The tariffs taxed imported manufactured goods, not the slave trade. This invents a mechanism that did not exist to make the slavery interpretation work.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. It reduces a constitutional crisis to personalities. Jackson and Calhoun did clash, but personal rivalry does not explain the doctrine of nullification or the tariff grievances behind it.
option_explanations.D: Right. It holds both interpretations at once: the tariffs were the real and immediate grievance, and the deeper fear was that federal tariff power implied federal power over slavery.

options: (A) The tariff-only interpretation is correct, because South Carolina's Ordinance of Nullification named the tariffs of 1828 and 1832 and said nothing about slavery, so slavery played no role in the crisis.
(B) The slavery interpretation is correct, because South Carolina nullified the tariffs in order to shield the slave trade from heavy federal taxation.
(C) Neither is correct: the crisis was really driven by the personal rivalry between Andrew Jackson and John C. Calhoun, which turned a routine policy dispute into a constitutional crisis.
(D) Each captures part of the truth: the tariffs were the immediate grievance, but South Carolina's leaders feared that yielding tariff power would open the way to federal action against slavery.
items.stem: One historian argues the nullification crisis was fundamentally about the tariff; another argues it was fundamentally about slavery. Which statement best evaluates these competing interpretations?

items.explanation: A sermon shows what the minister urged, not what listeners did — persuasion is not proof of changed behavior. The best test is behavioral evidence: pledge lists showing who actually signed, and consumption estimates showing whether drinking fell in revival towns. Membership rolls and reprint counts show reach, not results, and the minister's own memory is self-interested.
items.fact_source: Second Great Awakening revivals (1820s-1830s) fueled temperance organizing; historians test behavioral claims with pledge/membership records and alcohol-consumption estimates.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Joining a church is not the same as giving up drink. Membership rolls measure revival reach, not whether drinking behavior changed.
option_explanations.B: Right. Pledge lists record actual commitments and consumption estimates measure actual drinking — the behavioral evidence the claim about reduced drinking requires.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Wide reprinting shows the message traveled far; it does not show that anyone acted on it. The spread of an argument is not evidence the argument worked.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The minister had every reason to remember his own preaching as successful. A self-interested recollection is weaker than independent records of what people did.

options: (A) Church membership rolls showing how many new members joined congregations after revivals were held.
(B) Temperance society pledge lists and estimates of per-capita alcohol consumption in towns where revivals took place.
(C) The sermon's frequent reprinting, which shows that large numbers of Americans heard its message.
(D) The minister's autobiography, in which he recalls that hundreds signed temperance pledges after hearing him preach.
items.stem: A historian cites this sermon as evidence that the Second Great Awakening reduced drinking in American communities. Which additional evidence would best support that claim?

stimulus.text: An 1826 revival sermon urges listeners to give up drinking and sign a temperance pledge (paraphrased).

items.explanation: Calhoun delivered the 'positive good' speech as a political counterattack on abolitionists, not as a neutral description — it was designed to defend, so it cannot be read as a plain report of conditions. And the record contradicts the benevolent picture: the domestic slave trade forcibly moved roughly a million enslaved people, separating families, while enslaved people resisted in ways from sabotage to rebellion. Comparing slavery to Northern factory labor was itself part of the pro-slavery argument, not independent evidence.
items.fact_source: Calhoun 'positive good' speech, February 6, 1837; domestic ('second middle passage') slave trade moved about 1 million enslaved people, 1820s-1860; Nat Turner rebellion, 1831.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. His ownership does not make his plantation a valid stand-in for the whole South, and it misses the real problem: the speech was political defense, not a field report, wherever it was written.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Southerners stopped criticizing slavery because abolitionist attacks made open criticism politically dangerous, not because conditions improved. A change in rhetoric is not a change in conditions.
option_explanations.C: Right. It identifies the speech's defensive purpose — aimed at abolitionists — and brings outside evidence (forced family separation, resistance) that contradicts the benevolent portrait.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The 'wage slavery' comparison was itself a pro-slavery talking point. Accepting the comparison at face value repeats the argument instead of testing it.

options: (A) The speaker owned enslaved laborers himself, so only evidence drawn from his own plantation -- not abolitionist pamphlets -- could truly confirm or refute his description of slavery as a whole.
(B) After 1837 Southern writers largely stopped criticizing slavery in print, which strongly suggests that conditions for enslaved people must have improved.
(C) It was a political defense against abolitionist attacks, and the forced movement of about a million enslaved people through the domestic slave trade contradicts its benevolent picture.
(D) Because Northern factory workers also faced harsh and dangerous conditions, slavery was really no worse than the wage labor system of the North.
items.stem: A historian cites this speech to argue that slavery in the South was a benevolent institution. Which consideration most weakens that use of the speech?

stimulus.text: In an 1837 Senate speech, a Southern leader called slavery a 'positive good' that protected both Black and white Southerners (paraphrased).
